title: Hypersheaves on the Grothendieck total site as coherent sections
statement:
A small Grothendieck site is a small category with specified covering sieves, containing the maximal sieve and closed under pullback of sieves and transitivity; a sieve is a collection of arrows with fixed target closed under precomposition. A family covers when its generated sieve covers. No fibre products in the underlying category are required. All sizes use [def-weil-size-convention]. Let $\Lambda$ be a commutative ring and let $\mathbf D(\Lambda)$ be the enhanced localization of cochain complexes of $\Lambda$-modules at quasi-isomorphisms, retaining derived mapping complexes and all higher composition data [def-weil-abstract-derived-category, def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. A coherent presheaf is an enhanced functor $F:\mathcal C^{\mathrm{op}}\to\mathbf D(\Lambda)$ with the higher naturality data of [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. A $\mathbf D(\Lambda)$-valued hypersheaf is a coherent presheaf $F$ such that for every hypercover $T_\bullet\to T$ the map $F(T)\to\operatorname{holim}_{[n]\in\Delta}F(T_n)$ is an equivalence. Here a hypercover is an augmented simplicial family of representable presheaves whose maps to all matching presheaves are locally surjective after sheafification [def-weil-pbc-sheafification]; $F$ on a family is the product of its values. Write $\operatorname{Hyp}_{\ge a}(\mathcal C,\Lambda)$ for the full enhanced category of such $F$ with $H^i(F(T))=0$ for every $T$ and $i<a$, for a fixed integer $a$. Morphisms are coherent natural transformations, and mapping complexes are the derived ends in the coherent presheaf category.

Let $I$ be a small poset and $i\mapsto\mathcal C_i$ a strict covariant diagram of small Grothendieck sites. Each transition $\iota_{ij}:\mathcal C_i\to\mathcal C_j$, $i\le j$, is the inclusion of a full sieve: whenever an object of $\mathcal C_j$ maps to an object of $\mathcal C_i$, its source is also in $\mathcal C_i$. The topology on $\mathcal C_i$ is the restriction of the topology of $\mathcal C_j$; in particular covering sieves of objects of $\mathcal C_i$ are the same in the two sites. Assume the following local lower-refinement condition: whenever $i,j\le k$, $T\in\mathcal C_i$, $S\in\mathcal C_j$ and $S\to T$ is an arrow in $\mathcal C_k$, there is a covering family $\{S_\alpha\to S\}$ in $\mathcal C_j$ and indices $l_\alpha\le i,j$ such that $S_\alpha$ is in the image of $\mathcal C_{l_\alpha}\to\mathcal C_j$. Form the category $\mathcal E$ whose objects are $(i,T)$ with $T\in\mathcal C_i$, and whose morphisms $(i,T)\to(j,S)$ are $i\le j$ and an arrow $\iota_{ij}T\to S$ in $\mathcal C_j$. Give it the topology generated by vertical covering families in each $\mathcal C_i$ and by the singleton families $(i,T)\to(j,\iota_{ij}T)$ with underlying arrow the identity of $T$.

Restriction to the fibres identifies $\operatorname{Hyp}_{\ge a}(\mathcal E,\Lambda)$ with the enhanced homotopy limit
$$\operatorname{holim}_{i\in I^{\mathrm{op}}}\operatorname{Hyp}_{\ge a}(\mathcal C_i,\Lambda).$$
Thus the objects on the right are coherent systems $F_i$ with equivalences $\iota_{ij}^*F_j\simeq F_i$ and all composition homotopies. On the full subcategory of coherent presheaves on $\mathcal E$ that carry every indicated identity-underlying transition arrow to an equivalence, restriction identifies them with coherent sections of the fibre presheaf diagram equipped with the corresponding transition equivalences; the straightening comparison gives the inverse construction. Under this comparison the hypersheaf condition is exactly hyperdescent on every fibre together with inversion of these arrows. Derived mapping complexes on both sides are the same homotopy coherent ends over strings of arrows of $\mathcal E$, and the comparison respects composition. The equivalence is natural for inclusions of indexing posets and compatible diagrams of these sieve inclusions, and it preserves the pointwise lower bound $a$.

proof.text: Unpack the definitions of a small Grothendieck site, the generated topology on E, the enhanced derived target, and the pointwise lower-bound hypersheaf categories. The local lower-refinement condition is precisely the hypothesis needed when pulling a vertical cover across a mixed arrow; no fibre products of the underlying sites are used.

Apply the presheaf straightening lemma to the full subcategory of coherent presheaves that invert the identity-underlying transition arrows. Restriction gives the fibre presheaves and their coherent equivalences. Conversely, on an arrow $(i,T)\to(j,S)$, transport along the specified equivalence from $F_j(\iota_{ij}T)$ to $F_i(T)$ and then restrict along $\iota_{ij}(T)\to S$; strict functoriality and the coherence equations make this a presheaf and identify the two constructions up to coherent equivalence.

Use the local lower-refinement hyperdescent lemma for the topology generated by vertical covers and singleton transition arrows. Restricting a total hypersheaf to a fibre tests vertical hypercovers, while each singleton cover tests that its transition restriction map is an equivalence. Conversely, the lemma applies because the stated lower-refinement condition covers the sources of mixed arrows by objects indexed below both endpoints; it identifies the total hyperdescent map with the fibre descent maps together with those transition equivalences. Its pointwise formulation preserves the lower bound $a$.

Apply the coherent-end lemma to the presheaf equivalence. For coherent presheaves that invert the singleton transition arrows, the derived mapping complex is the homotopy-coherent end over strings of arrows in $\mathcal E$; after restricting each string to its fibre labels, this is the end defining maps of coherent systems. The construction is natural in both arguments, and the end composition law identifies identities and composites on the two sides.

The three comparisons are natural under a subposet inclusion or a compatible map of sieve diagrams: restriction preserves fibre objects, transition arrows, vertical covers, matching objects, and strings of arrows, and the inverse straightening and coherent-end formulas use only these operations. Therefore the hypersheaf equivalence, its lower-bound subcategories, and the mapping-complex identification commute with the stated restrictions and compatible maps.
